policy.uncertifiedDefault: Any sugya absent from records is UNCERTIFIED, regardless of legacy review metadata or historical audit findings.
policy.certification: CERTIFIED requires fresh sourceFingerprint and semanticFingerprint plus two fingerprint-bound source-first reviews with different reviewId values.
policy.repairProof: A first pass that finds REPAIR_REQUIRED cannot certify until repairRef exists and the live candidate differs from the first-pass reviewed fingerprints.
policy.invalidation: Any source, boundary, mapping, daf-summary, or semantic fingerprint change automatically makes the prior certificate STALE.
policy.bootstrapExit: Set strictMode true only after validate_semantic_certification.py --strict passes across the full corpus.

independentSourceReconstruction.method: Read authoritativeHebrewLines (vilna lines 1-39) in full before opening currentEnrichment. Reconstructed content independently from direct knowledge of the Mishnah/Gemara text at Yoma 2a.
flow: Lines 1-7 (Mishnah): Seven days before Yom Kippur the Kohen Gadol is moved from his house to the Parhedrin chamber; a backup priest is prepared in case of disqualification (pesul). Rabbi Yehuda: a backup wife should also be prepared, since 'u'v'ad beito' (Lev 16:6) means 'his wife', and if she dies before Yom Kippur he cannot serve. The Sages reject this: 'if so, there is no end to the matter' (ein la'davar sof - infinite regress).

Lines 8-13 (Gemara opens): Cites the parallel mishna from Parah (tractate Parah 3:1): seven days before the burning of the red heifer (parah adumah), the priest who burns it is likewise separated from his house to the chamber facing the Bira, northeast, called the Stone House (Lishkat Beit HaEven), because all its rites used vessels of dung, stone, and earth.

Lines 14-19: Explains why non-susceptible vessels were required: since a tevul yom (one who immersed that day but before sunset) is valid to burn the parah - contra the Sadducees, who held it must follow sunset after immersion (meorav shemesh) - the Sages would deliberately render the officiating priest tamei and immerse him publicly, to refute the Sadducean position. To prevent that public demonstration from breeding laxity about the parah's purity requirements generally, they mandated vessels immune to tumah (dung/stone/earth).

Lines 20-23: Explains why the chamber was northeast specifically: the parah is classified a chatat (sin-offering; Numbers 19:9,17), and a chatat's slaughter is associated with the north side; Numbers 19:4 requires the sprinkling 'el nokhach penei ohel mo'ed' (toward the front of the Tent of Meeting), i.e. facing east. Northeast satisfies both, and the location itself became a heikher (distinguishing indicator).

Lines 24-26: A short lexical dispute on the word 'bira' from the Parah mishna. Rabbi Yohanan (via Rabbah bar bar Chana): a specific named place on the Temple Mount. Reish Lakish: the term denotes the entire Temple complex, proven from David's phrase in Chronicles ('the bira I have prepared', I Chronicles 29:19); the citation itself (shene'emar ha'bira asher hakhinoti) physically prints on line 27, immediately continuing Reish Lakish's own sentence begun on line 26.

Lines 27-39: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the seven-day separation rule itself. Answer: Leviticus 8:34 (from the milu'im/Tabernacle-inauguration narrative), 'ka'asher asah bayom hazeh tzivah Hashem la'asot lechaper': 'la'asot' (to do) is read as the parah's actions, 'lechaper' (to atone) as Yom Kippur. Neither phrase can cover the whole verse alone (a parah does not atone; and without the gezerah shavah 'la'asot' has no proven referent for Yom Kippur), so the verse must split. A gezerah shavah on the shared word 'tzivah' links Lev 8:34 to Numbers 19:2 (the parah statute), formally proving 'la'asot' refers to the heifer and importing the seven-day sequestration requirement to it. Text is cut off mid-phrase at line 39 ('ve'eima...'), continuing on 2b.

evidence.boundaryNotes: All six declared lineRanges (1-7, 8-13, 14-19, 20-23, 24-26, 27-39) correspond to genuine topic units and match the natural Mishnah/Gemara paragraph breaks. One granularity note, not a defect: Reish Lakish's proof-text citation ('shene'emar ha'bira asher hakhinoti') is the printed continuation of his own statement (begun at line 26, s05) but physically falls on vilna line 27, which is s06's first line. This is an artifact of where the Vilna print happens to wrap the line, not semantic contamination - the fact asserted in s05 (Reish Lakish cites I Chronicles 29:19) is fully supported by the adjoining text and does not import content from a different topic or a different daf.
evidence.dafSummaryNotes: currentDafSummary accurately covers the page's throughline (Mishnah rule -> parah parallel -> stone-vessel reason -> northeast reason -> bira dispute -> gezerah shavah source). It omits the R. Yehuda/backup-wife dispute (lines 4-7) but states nothing false; a daf summary is a throughline, not an exhaustive index, and every fact it does state is source-supported.

perSugya.notes: Mishnah content (backup priest; R. Yehuda's backup-wife proposal from Lev 16:6 'u'v'ad beito'; Sages' infinite-regress rejection) matches source exactly. finalRuling ('A backup priest is designated; a backup wife is not') is the correct practical halacha per the Sages' rejected view of R. Yehuda. No content imported from elsewhere.

Parah mishna citation, Stone House name and its dung/stone/earth-vessel rule are all within lines 8-13. finalRuling's northeast reference is drawn from line 10's own text ('la'lishka she'al p'nei ha'bira tzafona mizracha'), not borrowed from s04's later explanation - factually stated, not fabricated.

Tevul-yom/Sadducee polemic matches lines 14-19 exactly: deliberate impurification-then-immersion as public refutation of the Sadducean 'meorav shemesh' position, then impervious vessels required so the demonstration doesn't breed purity laxity. No fabricated steps.
Chatat-requires-north + Numbers 19:4 'el nokhach penei ohel mo'ed'-requires-east = northeast, functioning as heikher, matches lines 20-23 exactly.

R. Yohanan/Reish Lakish 'bira' dispute matches lines 24-26 (plus the line-27 continuation of Reish Lakish's own sentence, see boundaryNotes). finalRuling correctly left empty since the dispute is unresolved on this daf.

Lev 8:34 split (la'asot/lechaper) and the tzivah/tzivah gezerah shavah to Numbers 19:2 matches lines 27-39 exactly, including the correct logical role of the gezerah shavah (proving 'la'asot' cannot mean Yom Kippur, forcing the split).

flow: Lines 1-6: Proposes and rejects two further 'tzivah' candidates for the gezerah shavah. First, Yom Kippur's own 'tzivah' (Lev 16:34, 'vaya'as ka'asher tzivah Hashem et Moshe') is rejected because it appears after the service was performed, not before, and a gezerah shavah requires matching functional position. Second, the offerings verse's 'tzavoto' (Num 28:2, 'beyom tzavoto et bnei Yisrael') is rejected because it is a different verb conjugation than 'tzivah', and identical forms are required when available.

Lines 7-10: A challenge from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: they derived a gezerah shavah between 'veshav' and 'uva' (Lev 14:39/44, leprous-house laws) despite those being different verb roots, so why can't 'tzavoto' pair with 'tzivah'? Answer: that method applies only when no identical form is available; here 'tzivah' itself is available in the heifer passage (Num 19), so the identical form must be used.

Lines 11-16: Narrows 'lechaper' (to atone). Could it mean atonement offerings generally? A practical objection (we don't know in advance which kohen serves) is rebutted (the whole mishmeret/beit av rotation is known in advance and could be required to separate) - so the real exclusion is a different principle: we derive a time-fixed matter (the inauguration) from another time-fixed matter (Yom Kippur), excluding daily offerings which recur every day with no fixed annual date.

flow: Lines 1-6: Proposes and rejects two further 'tzivah' candidates for the gezerah shavah. First, Yom Kippur's own 'tzivah' (Lev 16:34, 'vaya'as ka'asher tzivah Hashem et Moshe') is rejected because it appears after the service was performed, not before, and a gezerah shavah requires matching functional position. Second, the offerings verse's 'tzavoto' (Num 28:2, 'beyom tzavoto et bnei Yisrael') is rejected because it is a different verb conjugation than 'tzivah', and identical forms are required when available.

Lines 7-10: A challenge from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: they derived a gezerah shavah between 'veshav' and 'uva' (Lev 14:39/44, leprous-house laws) despite those being different verb roots, so why can't 'tzavoto' pair with 'tzivah'? Answer: that method applies only when no identical form is available; here 'tzivah' itself is available in the heifer passage (Num 19), so the identical form must be used.

Lines 11-16: Narrows 'lechaper' (to atone). Could it mean atonement offerings generally? A practical objection (we don't know in advance which kohen serves) is rebutted (the whole mishmeret/beit av rotation is known in advance and could be required to separate) - so the real exclusion is a different principle: we derive a time-fixed matter (the inauguration) from another time-fixed matter (Yom Kippur), excluding daily offerings which recur every day with no fixed annual date.

Lines 16-19: Could it mean Festival service? Excluded because we derive a once-a-year matter from a once-a-year matter; Festivals (Pesach/Sukkot) occur three times a year via their pilgrimage cycle, not once.

Lines 19-23: Could it mean one specific Festival (Chag HaMatzot, since Scripture opens with it first; or Chag HaSukkot, since it has more commandments - sukkah, lulav, water libation)? Excluded structurally: we derive a seven-day separation for a one-day service from a seven-day separation for a one-day service; a Festival's own service spans seven days, so deriving 'seven-for-seven' from 'seven-for-one' is invalid.

Lines 23-28: Could it mean Shemini Atzeret specifically (seven days of Sukkot preceding one culminating day)? Excluded because we derive a case with no sanctity preceding it (the inauguration, ordinary days before) from another case with no preceding sanctity (Yom Kippur); Shemini Atzeret is preceded by seven holy days of Sukkot. A kal va-chomer is proposed (if a case without preceding sanctity needs separation, surely one with preceding sanctity needs it more) and rejected twice: Rav Mesharshiyya ('lo hazeh ketiv, kazeh' - the verse says 'kazeh' [like this], limiting the derivation to cases structurally matching the inauguration, not extending it further by kal va-chomer); Rav Ashi (the primary Festival, Sukkot itself, needs no separation, so its appendage cannot be stricter - and this holds even for the view that Shemini Atzeret is fully independent).
Line 29 onward (into 3a): the mnemonic 'PZR KSHB' begins, continuing past this daf's raw text window.

independentSourceReconstruction.method: Read authoritativeHebrewLines (vilna lines 1-20) in full before opening currentEnrichment.
flow: Line 1: The PZR KSHB mnemonic (Payis/lottery, Zeman/shehecheyanu, Regel/festival-status, Korban/offering-count, Shira/song, Berakhah/prayer) - six respects in which Shemini Atzeret is independent of Sukkot. But for tashlumin (compensation offerings), it still counts as Sukkot's own last day, proven from the Sukkah mishna that a missed festival offering may be brought through the whole festival including its final day.
Lines 2-3: Continuation/proof-citation for the tashlumin point (the Sukkah mishna quoted in full).

Lines 4-15: Rabbi Abba excludes Shavuot (Atzeret) via offering profile: Yom Kippur and the inauguration both bring one bull and one ram; Shavuot brings two rams. Challenge: R. Eliezer b. R. Shimon holds Yom Kippur itself has two rams (one from Acharei Mot/Leviticus, one from Pinchas/Numbers) - so what distinguishes it from Shavuot? Resolution: even so, Yom Kippur's two rams serve different functions (one is chovat hayom/day-obligation, the other is mussaf), while Shavuot's two rams (per the Two Loaves verse) are both chovat hayom. The functional mismatch, not mere count, excludes Shavuot.

Lines 16-20: Rabbi Abbahu excludes Rosh Hashana (and re-excludes Shavuot on a second ground) via property source: Yom Kippur's and the inauguration's bull-and-ram both come from the Kohen Gadol's own property ('kach lecha' - take for yourself), while Rosh Hashana's and Shavuot's come from communal funds. This works for the view that 'kach lecha' means personal property; the daf closes mid-word ('ve'aseh...') raising the alternative view, continuing on 3b.

flow: Lines 1-15: Completes the kach-lecha/aseh-lecha dispute. R. Yoshiya: both phrases mean personal property; R. Yonatan: both mean communal, but God expresses a preference for Moses's personal contribution ('kevayachol, I want yours more than theirs'). Abba Chanan (in R. Elazar's name) resolves the Ark-verse contradiction (Deut 10:1 singular vs. Exod 25:10 plural) by context, not grammar: when Israel obeys, the work is credited to them. Lines 12-19: the Gemara sidesteps the whole general dispute for THIS case - within the same divine speech, the phrasing itself shifts from communal ('kechu se'ir izim') to personal ('kach lecha egel'), and the contrast itself (not the general rule) proves personal property at the inauguration.

Lines 20-27: The same proof applied to Yom Kippur: Leviticus 16 first commands taking two goats 'from the community' then says 'his bull' - the contrast proves personal property. Rav Ashi offers an independent structural exclusion: derive bull-chatat+ram-olah (YK) from bull-chatat+ram-olah (inauguration), excluding Rosh Hashana and Shavuot (both olot only).

Lines 28-34: Ravina offers two further independent exclusions: (v1) derive Kohen-Gadol-restricted service from Kohen-Gadol-restricted service; (v2, after disambiguating what 'techilah'/initial means) derive initial service in the sacred place from initial service in the sacred place - the eighth day of the inauguration (first service at the outer altar) and the first Yom Kippur (first entry into the Holy of Holies).

Lines 35-45 (through amar lei Reish Lakish): Rav Dimi reports R. Yochanan taught only one case (YK) from 'la'asot, lechaper'; R. Yehoshua ben Levi taught two (heifer + YK). Challenge: the mishna itself lists both heifer and YK sequestering - so how can R. Yochanan hold one case? Answer: heifer sequestering is a rabbinic maaleh (a compensating stringency for the Sages' tvul-yom leniency), not Torah-derived. Further challenge: a chain via R. Minyumi bar Chilkiya/R. Machseya bar Idi cites R. Yochanan HIMSELF teaching two cases (the exact quote already reviewed as part of yoma-002a-s06's own content). Resolution: that was R. Yochanan transmitting HIS TEACHER R. Yishmael's view, not his own; Ravin's report from Eretz Yisrael confirms R. Yochanan's personal position is one case.

Lines 45-53: Reish Lakish challenges R. Yochanan directly ('a"l Reish Lakish leRabbi Yochanan: meheicha ka'ilfat lah? Mimeluim?'): if YK-sequestration derives from the inauguration, everything written there should be indispensable for YK's validity. In ONE CONTINUOUS SPEECH (no intervening 'amar lei' until line 50's 'ela mar meheicha yalif lah'), Reish Lakish then preempts and refutes two possible defenses: (a) 'and if you would say indeed so [everything IS indispensable]' - but the mishna itself says 'they DESIGNATE (matkin) another priest' for the backup, not 'they SEPARATE (mafrishin) him' - proving sequestering is not indispensable even for the backup case; (b) 'and if you would say matkin just means mafrishin' - then the mishna should have used the SAME word for both KG and backup, not two different words. This whole chain (lines 46-50, ending '...mafrishin') is Reish Lakish's own uninterrupted argument. Only then ('a"l', line 50) does Rabbi Yochanan speak, turning the question back: 'Then where do YOU derive it from?' Reish Lakish answers: from Sinai - Exodus 24:16, the cloud covered Moses six days before God called him on the seventh, teaching that entering the Divine Presence requires six days' preparation. The daf closes on the obvious challenge: our mishna requires seven days, not six (resolved on 4a via R. Yehuda ben Beteira's niddah concern).

flow: Lines 1-15: Completes the kach-lecha/aseh-lecha dispute. R. Yoshiya: both phrases mean personal property; R. Yonatan: both mean communal, but God expresses a preference for Moses's personal contribution ('kevayachol, I want yours more than theirs'). Abba Chanan (in R. Elazar's name) resolves the Ark-verse contradiction (Deut 10:1 singular vs. Exod 25:10 plural) by context, not grammar: when Israel obeys, the work is credited to them. Lines 12-19: the Gemara sidesteps the whole general dispute for THIS case - within the same divine speech, the phrasing itself shifts from communal ('kechu se'ir izim') to personal ('kach lecha egel'), and the contrast itself (not the general rule) proves personal property at the inauguration.

Lines 20-27: The same proof applied to Yom Kippur: Leviticus 16 first commands taking two goats 'from the community' then says 'his bull' - the contrast proves personal property. Rav Ashi offers an independent structural exclusion: derive bull-chatat+ram-olah (YK) from bull-chatat+ram-olah (inauguration), excluding Rosh Hashana and Shavuot (both olot only).

Lines 28-34: Ravina offers two further independent exclusions: (v1) derive Kohen-Gadol-restricted service from Kohen-Gadol-restricted service; (v2, after disambiguating what 'techilah'/initial means) derive initial service in the sacred place from initial service in the sacred place - the eighth day of the inauguration (first service at the outer altar) and the first Yom Kippur (first entry into the Holy of Holies).

Lines 35-45 (through amar lei Reish Lakish): Rav Dimi reports R. Yochanan taught only one case (YK) from 'la'asot, lechaper'; R. Yehoshua ben Levi taught two (heifer + YK). Challenge: the mishna itself lists both heifer and YK sequestering - so how can R. Yochanan hold one case? Answer: heifer sequestering is a rabbinic maaleh (a compensating stringency for the Sages' tvul-yom leniency), not Torah-derived. Further challenge: a chain via R. Minyumi bar Chilkiya/R. Machseya bar Idi cites R. Yochanan HIMSELF teaching two cases (the exact quote already reviewed as part of yoma-002a-s06's own content). Resolution: that was R. Yochanan transmitting HIS TEACHER R. Yishmael's view, not his own; Ravin's report from Eretz Yisrael confirms R. Yochanan's personal position is one case.

Lines 45-53: Reish Lakish challenges R. Yochanan directly ('a"l Reish Lakish leRabbi Yochanan: meheicha ka'ilfat lah? Mimeluim?'): if YK-sequestration derives from the inauguration, everything written there should be indispensable for YK's validity. In ONE CONTINUOUS SPEECH (no intervening 'amar lei' until line 50's 'ela mar meheicha yalif lah'), Reish Lakish then preempts and refutes two possible defenses: (a) 'and if you would say indeed so [everything IS indispensable]' - but the mishna itself says 'they DESIGNATE (matkin) another priest' for the backup, not 'they SEPARATE (mafrishin) him' - proving sequestering is not indispensable even for the backup case; (b) 'and if you would say matkin just means mafrishin' - then the mishna should have used the SAME word for both KG and backup, not two different words. This whole chain (lines 46-50, ending '...mafrishin') is Reish Lakish's own uninterrupted argument. Only then ('a"l', line 50) does Rabbi Yochanan speak, turning the question back: 'Then where do YOU derive it from?' Reish Lakish answers: from Sinai - Exodus 24:16, the cloud covered Moses six days before God called him on the seventh, teaching that entering the Divine Presence requires six days' preparation. The daf closes on the obvious challenge: our mishna requires seven days, not six (resolved on 4a via R. Yehuda ben Beteira's niddah concern).

flow: Lines 1: Completes 3b's cutoff word 'letumat beito' (concerning the impurity of his household - R. Yehuda ben Beteira's niddah concern, resolving the seven-vs-six challenge).

Lines 1-9: R. Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish: his (Yochanan's) inauguration-derivation explains the sprinkling requirement (there WAS sprinkling at the inauguration, per a baraita: both the KG and heifer-priest are sprinkled all seven days from the ashes/sin-offerings kept there); but Reish Lakish's Sinai-derivation has no sprinkling at all - was there sprinkling at Sinai? Reish Lakish counters: even Yochanan's own derivation has a problem - inauguration sprinkling was BLOOD, current practice is WATER. Rabbi Chiya's principle (water replaced blood, taught elsewhere in this same discussion, i.e. later in the sugya per Rashi) bridges that medium gap for R. Yochanan. But Reish Lakish has no equivalent bridge for a complete ABSENCE of sprinkling at Sinai, and concedes: the sprinkling itself is just a maaleh (rabbinic enhancement) that cannot be derived from his source.

Lines 9-34: A baraita supports R. Yochanan: Leviticus 16:3's 'bezot' (with this, feminine) - since the immediately following offerings (bull, ram) are masculine, the feminine form is grammatically surplus, signaling it points instead to 'what is stated in the matter' (the inauguration context): Aaron withdrew seven days and Moses personally trained him in the service all seven days. By extension for future generations: the Kohen Gadol withdraws seven days and is served/trained by two Torah scholars from among Moses's disciples (explicitly excluding Sadducees, who rejected the transmitted Oral Torah). Since bull/ram alone don't need the feminine 'bezot' (a masculine/plural form would suffice), the feminine surplus teaches TWO things: the specific offerings AND the sequestering practice. A further verse (Lev 8:34's 'ka'asher asah bayom hazeh') extends the obligation from Aaron's own inaugural Yom Kippur to all future High Priests and Yom Kippurs, addressing an objection that it might apply only to that first, inaugural Yom Kippur or only to Aaron personally.

Lines 35-42 (continuing to 4b): A baraita supports Reish Lakish's Sinai derivation: Moses ascended into the cloud, was covered by cloud, and was sanctified in cloud in order to receive the Torah for Israel in holiness, as it is written 'and the glory of the LORD rested on Mount Sinai and the cloud covered it six days, and He called to Moses on the seventh day' (Exodus 24:16). A dispute follows over WHEN these six days occurred: R. Yosi HaGalili holds this was AFTER the Ten Commandments were given, at the start of the forty-day period when Moses ascended to receive the tablets; R. Akiva holds it was BEFORE the Ten Commandments, from Rosh Chodesh Sivan until the Torah was given on the seventh day. Text is cut off mid-verse at 'vayechasehu' (and it covered him), continuing on 4b.

independentSourceReconstruction.method: Read authoritativeHebrewLines (vilna lines 1-47) in full before opening currentEnrichment.
flow: Lines 1-9: Three tannaitic readings of the six-day cloud (continuing R. Akiva's view from 4a's baraita): R. Akiva - the cloud covered the mountain, not Moses; the public calling honored Moses. R. Natan - the cloud purged food/drink from Moses's system so he could go 40 days without eating, like a ministering angel. R. Matya ben Charash - the cloud instilled awe so Torah would be received with trembling. Rav Adda bar Mattana citing Rav adds Psalm 2's 'serve God with awe and rejoice with trembling' - joy and trembling coexist.

Lines 11-27: Calendar dispute. R. Yosi HaGalili holds like the anonymous first Tanna (Torah given 6 Sivan); R. Akiva holds like 'Rabbi Yosi' from the same baraita (Torah given 7 Sivan, ascended same day). Tested against the tradition that the tablets broke 17 Tammuz after 40 days on the mountain: R. Akiva's count (7 Sivan start, 24 remaining days of Sivan + 16 of Tammuz = 40) lands exactly on 17 Tammuz. R. Yosi HaGalili's count (6 Sivan Torah-giving, then 6 more separation days, ascending ~13 Sivan, +40) would land around 23 Tammuz unless the six separation days are counted as part of (not additional to) the forty mountain days - which the Gemara says he holds. The passage then notes 'vayikra el Moshe, Moshe, and all Israel stood' supports 'Rabbi Elazar' (unqualified in the source - no 'ben Azariah'), who taught this verse's repetition/staging was solely to honor Moses.

Lines 29-36: A contradiction (public voice at Sinai vs. private 'kol lo' at the Tent of Meeting) resolved by distinguishing the public call (kria) from the private content (dibbur). A second problem: how did Moses enter the cloud-blocked Tent? Rabbi Elazar (same sage as above, unqualified) says God pulled him in; the school of Rabbi Yishmael derives via gezerah shavah from the sea-crossing ('betoch') that Moses walked through an opening, not immersion. Two practical rules follow from 'vayikra...vayedaber' and 'lemor': always call before speaking (echoed by, not originated from, Rabbi Chanina's independent teaching), and 'lemor' read as 'lo emor' teaches confidentiality until permission is given (Rabbah, per the primary reading of a textually bracketed/uncertain attribution in the source).

Lines 41-47: 'Vayedaber Hashem eilav me'ohel moed lemor' implies both parties of the earlier exchange (Reish Lakish and R. Yochanan, from 3b-4a) treat everything written about the inauguration as indispensable. This connects to an independently reported dispute: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina disagree - one holds everything written in the inauguration is indispensable, the other holds only what is also indispensable for the ongoing/future service is indispensable in the inauguration itself. Since R. Yochanan's earlier silence (in the matkin/mafrishin exchange, already reviewed and repaired on 3b) already committed him to 'everything is indispensable,' he must be the strict position; R. Chanina holds the narrower view. The daf ends with the open question of their practical difference, continuing to 5a.

Matya ben Charash - the cloud instilled awe so Torah would be received with trembling. Akiva holds like 'Rabbi Yosi' from the same baraita (Torah given 7 Sivan, ascended same day). Tested against the tradition that the tablets broke 17 Tammuz after 40 days on the mountain: R. flow: Lines 1-9: Rav Yosef names semikha (hand-laying) as a practical difference between R. Yochanan and R. Chanina, proven not to invalidate ongoing service via a baraita on Lev. 1:4 ('vesamach...venirtza') read against Lev. 17:11 (only blood atones) - semikha is a shirei mitzva.
Lines 10-18: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak names tenufah (waving), with the identical baraita structure for its own verse.
Lines 18-23: Rav Pappa names prishat shivah (seven-day separation), proven via the mishna's word choice 'matkinin' (they designate) rather than 'mafrishin' (they separate) for the backup priest.
Line 23: Ravina opens the second sugya by naming two more differences: ribui shivah (seven days of increased/full garments) and meshichah shivah (seven days of anointing).

Lines 24-34: A baraita on Lev. 16:32 ('vechiper hakohen asher yimshach... ve'asher yemale et yado') teaches that any combination of seven-day garment-wearing and seven-day anointing suffices (not only both together, as the base case from Exod. 29:30 might have suggested). The Gemara then asks the source for meshichah shivah being required lechatchila (ab initio), given we already know ribui shivah is lechatchila from Exod. 29:30 itself.

Lines 35-37: Two answers are offered for meshichah shivah lechatchila: (1) 'im ba'it eima, from the fact a verse was needed to exclude/limit' (a terse first answer the current enrichment omits entirely), and (2) 'im ba'it eima, a hekesh (juxtaposition) from Exod. 29:29 (vivgdei hakodesh asher le'Aharon...) linking anointing to garment-wearing: just as garment-wearing is seven days, so is anointing.

Lines 38-40 (daf ends mid-word): R. Yitzchak bar Bisna gives the source for R. Yochanan's entire principle (that everything written in the inauguration invalidates): the word 'kachah' (thus) in Exodus 29:35 ('ve'asita le'Aharon ulevanav kachah'). The Gemara notes this works for anything ('tinach kol milta') written in the inauguration passage itself - and cuts off, continuing on 5b to ask about requirements written elsewhere.

flow: Lines 1-5: The stub question from 5a's end is restated. Three Amoraim bridge the Exodus-kachah gap to Leviticus inauguration requirements: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak via gezerah shavah on the repeated word 'petach' (opening); Rav Mesharshiya from the inclusive phrase 'u-shmartem et mishmeret Hashem' (Lev. 8:35); Rav Ashi from 'ki chen tzuviti' (also in Lev. 8:35) as a blanket warrant.

Lines 5-9: A baraita distinguishes three near-identical phrases that recur across Lev. 8-10: 'ki chen tzuviti' (a separate occurrence, Lev. 10:12, re: the eighth-day meal-offering) teaches Aaron may eat the offering despite being an onen (acute mourner, Nadav and Avihu having just died); 'ka'asher tziviti' (Lev. 10:13) marks that Moses spoke this instruction at the moment of discovering the burned sin-offering goat; 'ka'asher tzivah Hashem' (Lev. 10:15) establishes Moses was relaying God's command, not his own ruling.

Lines 9-15: R. Yosei bar Chanina derives that trousers (not written in the implementation/dressing passage) are included via the inclusive prefix 've-zeh hadavar' (Exod. 29:1); the tenth-of-an-ephah is derived by gezerah shavah on the word 'zeh' from Lev. 6:13 ('zeh korban Aharon uvanav... asirit ha'eifah'). R. Yochanan, citing R. Shimon ben Yochai, derives that even reading the passage aloud was indispensable, from 'zeh hadavar' in the verse describing Moses addressing the congregation.

Lines 19-24: The redundant phrase 'how did he dress them, how did he dress them' is reframed: not historical curiosity (what happened, happened) nor a future-practice question (Moses will know when Aaron and sons return), but a textual harmonization problem. The sons of R. Chiya and R. Yochanan disagree whether Moses dressed Aaron first, then his sons, or all together. Abaye (starting mid-line-25) clarifies that for the tunic and mitre everyone agrees Aaron came first (both command and implementation texts list Aaron first); the dispute is only about the belt.

Lines 25-31: The actual proof-texts for each position, NOT currently captured with explicit sourceRefs in the enrichment: the 'Aaron then sons' position relies on the implementation verses (Lev. 8:7 'vayachgor oto ba'avnet' - he girded HIM, Aaron alone; then Lev. 8:13 'vayachgor otam avnet' - he girded THEM, the sons - i.e. sequential, matching sequential dressing). The 'together' position relies on the command verse (Exod. 29:9 'vechagarta otam' - you shall gird THEM - a single combined form for Aaron and sons together).

Lines 32-34 (daf ends mid-word): A challenge is raised specifically against the 'together' position: but doesn't the implementation ALSO say 'he girded him' (Aaron alone) and then separately 'he girded them' (sons) - the same sequential language used to support the OTHER position? The Gemara's answer ('amar' - '[X] said') is cut off; the daf ends here and the resolution continues on 6a.

flow: Lines 1-8: The 5b belt-sequence challenge is resolved. The 'together' position explains the two implementation verses (Lev 8:7 'he girded him', 8:13 'he girded them') as teaching material difference (High Priest's belt is kilaim, wool-linen mix, from Exodus 39:29; ordinary priest's belt is plain linen), not sequence. The 'Aaron first' position explains the command's combined 've-chagarta otam' (Exod 29:9) as teaching material identity (both kilaim), leaving the two implementation verses to prove sequential dressing. The Gemara asks why two verses are needed if belts are identical, and whether five people can really be girded 'at once' - answered: 'bvat achat' means one continuous, uninterrupted operation (Moses dressed everyone except belts, then returned to gird Aaron then the sons), not literal simultaneity.

Lines 8-14: New mishna topic: why does the Kohen Gadol leave his home (his wife), not just enter the Parhedrin chamber? R. Yehuda ben Beteira's baraita, as initially cited, says the concern is that his wife might be found a safek niddah and then he comes to her. The Gemara objects: that implies knowing wickedness. The corrected reading: he comes to her innocently, and she is found a safek niddah afterward (blood discovered on the sheets, creating retroactive seven-day impurity uncertainty).

Lines 15-21: The Sages assume this safek niddah concern only follows R. Akiva (who holds a niddah retroactively impurifies her partner); the Rabbis, who reject this, would see no problem. Rav Chisda corrects: even the Rabbis agree when blood is found 'chad achar' (immediately, within the time to get up and wash); they only disagree with R. Akiva regarding 'achar achar' (a longer delay). R. Zeira then draws a general conclusion from this discussion: a bo'el niddah is not like a niddah and immerses by day, not at night.

Lines 21-26: R. Zeira's impossibility proof: if bo'el niddah had to immerse at night like a niddah, and his seventh day of separation fell on Yom Kippur eve, he would immerse Yom Kippur night - but he then needs sunset ('he'erev hashemesh') to complete purification, and that sunset is Yom Kippur itself, too late to serve. Therefore bo'el niddah must be able to immerse by day.

Lines 26-28: Rav Shimi from Neharde'a offers an alternative that doesn't require daytime immersion: separate the Kohen Gadol slightly before sunset eight days before Yom Kippur (rather than a full eight days), so the seventh day completes before Yom Kippur night even under a nighttime-immersion rule.

Lines 28-35 (daf ends mid-word): Two baraitot challenge R. Zeira's daytime-immersion ruling. Baraita 1: all who immerse do so by day, except niddah/yoledet who immerse at night - implying bo'el niddah (unlisted) immerses by day; deflected because the baraita's 'niddah' category includes anyone whose impurity derives from her, i.e., bo'el niddah too. Baraita 2: bo'el niddah is compared to tamei met (seven-day impurity) as ba'al keri is compared to one who touched a sheretz (one-day impurity) - does this teach daytime immersion? Deflected: the comparison is only about impurity duration, both of which are independently explicit in Torah verses; the Gemara asks what the comparison then teaches, cutting off mid-word ('ela'), continuing on 6b.

flow: Lines 1-4: 6a's open question (what does baraita 2's tamei-met comparison teach, if not immersion timing) is answered: it teaches that bo'el niddah is actually MORE severe than tamei met in one respect - he transmits mishkav/moshav impurity (a mild impurity rendering food/drink impure), which tamei met does not.

Lines 4-7: R. Chiyya's baraita is cited as a decisive proof (teyuvta): zav, zava, metzora, metzora'at, bo'el niddah, and tamei met all immerse by day; niddah and yoledet immerse at night. Bo'el niddah is explicitly listed among the daytime immersers, conclusively settling 6a's R. Zeira/baraita dispute.

Lines 7-13: New question: if the Kohen Gadol is separated from his wife to prevent niddah impurity, why not also separate him from visitors who might die and convey corpse impurity? Rav Tachlifa (in Rava's name): the omission proves tumas met is fully permitted (hutrah) for communal service. Ravina's counter: even if only overridden (dchuya), corpse impurity from a visitor is rare while niddah impurity is a common, everyday risk - explaining the asymmetric legislation without conceding hutrah.

Lines 14-24 (daf ends mid-word): The hutrah/dchuya question becomes a formal, independently-stated amoraic dispute: Rav Nachman holds tumas met is hutrah for the community, Rav Sheshet holds it is dchuya. The Gemara clarifies scope: both agree that within a single beit av (priestly division), pure priests serve and impure ones do not; they disagree only about summoning pure priests from a different beit av when the whole division is impure - Rav Nachman (hutrah) says no need to fetch, Rav Sheshet (dchuya) says fetch them. A second version (ika de'amrei) escalates further: even within the SAME beit av where both pure and impure priests are present, Rav Nachman holds the impure ones may also serve, since tumas met is simply inapplicable to communal service. The daf cuts off mid-word ('dechol'), continuing on 7a.

independentSourceReconstruction.method: Read authoritativeHebrewLines (vilna lines 1-18) in full before opening currentEnrichment.
flow: Lines 1-2: completes 7a's cutoff - the tzitz bears only the sin of tumah, which was permitted (hutrah) for the community; this is a difficulty (kashya) for Rav Sheshet's dchuya position.

Lines 2-10: A tannaitic baraita is cited to resolve this as a matter of dispute (tannai hi). Rabbi SHIMON holds the tzitz atones whether on the forehead or not. Rabbi YEHUDA holds it only atones while still on the forehead. Rabbi SHIMON then says to Rabbi Yehuda: let the Yom Kippur Kohen Gadol prove it - he serves without the tzitz on his forehead (during the inner sanctum service in white linen) and yet atonement occurs. Rabbi YEHUDA responds: leave aside the Yom Kippur Kohen Gadol, for there tumah was fully permitted (hutrah) to him for the sake of the community [so no proof about the tzitz's normal function can be drawn from a case where it isn't even operating]. By inference: Rabbi SHIMON holds tumah is generally overridden (dchuya) for the community [since he did not treat Yom Kippur as an unremarkable case needing no tzitz-atonement, and his position rests on the tzitz having a real, general atoning function].

Lines 11-18: Abaye localizes the tannaitic dispute: when the tzitz is broken, all agree it does not atone; the actual dispute is only when it hangs on a peg (intact, off the forehead). R. Yehuda's position rests on 'al mitzcho v'nasa' (fitness for the forehead required); R. Shimon's on 'tamid l'ratzon lifnei Hashem' (perpetual atonement). flow: Lines 1-4: completes 7b's cutoff kal v'chomer - the tzitz (one divine name) requires constant mindfulness, so tefillin (many divine names) certainly do too.

Lines 4-13: source-derivation audit for R. Shimon and R. Yehuda's positions established on 7b. R. Shimon (challenged: doesn't 'al mitzcho v'nasa' require forehead placement, contradicting his 'tamid=perpetual atonement' view?) answers that verse merely fixes the normal location, not an atonement condition; asked what the extra word 'v'nasa' then teaches, he derives 'ravui lamitzach' (fit for the forehead atones, unfit - i.e. broken - does not). R. Yehuda derives the forehead-placement requirement from 'al mitzcho' directly, and the broken-tzitz exclusion from a separate doubled 'mitzcho/mitzcho' across two verses; R. Shimon does not use that doubling since he already derived the broken-tzitz rule from 'v'nasa'.

Lines 14-20: a baraita on hazaah (sprinkling): R. Meir - both the YK Kohen Gadol and the para-aduma priest are sprinkled all seven separation days; R. Yosei - only day 3 and day 7 for both; R. Chanina Segan HaKohanim - the para priest gets all seven, the YK Kohen Gadol only day 3 and 7.
Lines 21-25: first hypothesis - the dispute maps onto dchuya (R. Meir) vs. hutrah (R. Yosei) - rejected: if R. Yosei held hutrah, he would require no sprinkling at all, not specifically day 3 and 7.

Lines 25-34: second hypothesis - both hold dchuya; dispute is whether 'tevila bizmana mitzva' (immersion at its proper time is a mitzva) - R. Meir yes, R. Yosei no. Challenged and rejected via a cross-tractate baraita (a person with God's Name tattooed on his skin): the tanna kama's cautious method (wrapping a reed before immersing) reflects NOT holding tevila-bizmana-mitzva, while R. Yosei's own ruling (immerse normally, just don't rub) reflects that he DOES hold tevila bizmana is a mitzva - directly contradicting the second hypothesis's premise that R. Yosei denies it.

Lines 34-39: third and correct resolution - both hold tevila bizmana mitzva; the real dispute is whether hazaah is EQUATED to tevila for timing purposes: R. Meir yes (so sprinkle every day, since any day might be the halakhic 'proper' one), R. Yosei no (sprinkle only the Torah-specified day 3 and 7). This resolution creates a new problem for R. Chanina Segan's split ruling, since a simple binary equate/don't-equate reading would give both priests the SAME ruling.

Lines 39-41 (daf ends mid-citation): resolved - R. Chanina Segan does not equate hazaah to tevila at all; the para priest's all-seven-day sprinkling is merely an elevated stringency (ma'alah b'alma), unrelated to the timing-equation principle. The daf then begins introducing a supporting citation ('there is no difference between the priest who burns the heifer and the Kohen Gadol on Yom Kippur except that this...') which cuts off after a single word, continuing to 8b.

Lines 21-25: first hypothesis - the dispute maps onto dchuya (R. Meir) vs. hutrah (R. Yosei) - rejected: if R. Yosei held hutrah, he would require no sprinkling at all, not specifically day 3 and 7.

Lines 25-34: second hypothesis - both hold dchuya; dispute is whether 'tevila bizmana mitzva' (immersion at its proper time is a mitzva) - R. Meir yes, R. Yosei no. Challenged and rejected via a cross-tractate baraita (a person with God's Name tattooed on his skin): the tanna kama's cautious method (wrapping a reed before immersing) reflects NOT holding tevila-bizmana-mitzva, while R. Yosei's own ruling (immerse normally, just don't rub) reflects that he DOES hold tevila bizmana is a mitzva - directly contradicting the second hypothesis's premise that R. Yosei denies it.

Lines 34-39: third and correct resolution - both hold tevila bizmana mitzva; the real dispute is whether hazaah is EQUATED to tevila for timing purposes: R. Meir yes (so sprinkle every day, since any day might be the halakhic 'proper' one), R. Yosei no (sprinkle only the Torah-specified day 3 and 7). This resolution creates a new problem for R. Chanina Segan's split ruling, since a simple binary equate/don't-equate reading would give both priests the SAME ruling.

Lines 39-41 (daf ends mid-citation): resolved - R. Chanina Segan does not equate hazaah to tevila at all; the para priest's all-seven-day sprinkling is merely an elevated stringency (ma'alah b'alma), unrelated to the timing-equation principle. Because Yochanan High Priest sent emissaries throughout Israel and saw that only terumah gedolah was being universally separated (Rashi cross-references this decree to Sotah 48a). Ulla then explains: since the parhedrin officials already beat the bakers every 12 months demanding cheap sales, the Rabbis did not burden them with this maaser sheni requirement on top of that pressure. A brief etymological gloss follows ('what are parhedrin? cavalry/horsemen').
